New UC Berkeley and Microsoft paper cuts coding-agent token costs by 18.4% to 30.9% using an external controller that learns from past runs.

by injecting learned facts, pruning unused tools, and stopping failed loops early.

Coding agents are billed by the token, and each turn resends the growing history, so long projects get expensive. Token efficiency is usually measured on isolated tasks, missing the cost that builds up across a sequence of tasks in the same codebase.

TokenEconomizer sits outside the agent as a black box, changing only prompts and tool settings. From past runs it learns which facts to inject, which unused tools to drop, and when to stop a failing loop.

Across Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot CLI on 277 SWE-Bench tasks, it cut mean per-task cost 18.4% to 30.9%. It improved Pass@1 in 4 of 5 agent-model settings, and savings held in every repository.

Measure agent cost across a whole project, not per task, and use an external controller that adapts to each repo, not fixed plugins.

note_tweet.text:
This survey argues that self-improvement tricks for multimodal agents only carry over to tasks that have what the trick relies on, like checkable answers.

AI agent learn from its own attempts in 1 area, like questions about images, can fail in another, like robotics, where there is nothing to check.

Self-improving agents now span visual reasoning, image generation, app and web navigation, and robotics, but each method is tested in only 1 setting. Majority voting, for example, scores short visual answers but finds nothing to compare in robot action trajectories.

The author reviewed methods in the 4 settings and listed each trick's needs, like answers a vote can compare or results a program can check. Each trick then gets a verdict per setting: portable, conditional, blocked, or redundant.

In 1 cited audit of 500 questions, 24% of kept majority-vote labels were wrong, against 5.6% for program-computed answers. These verdicts are predictions, not results from transfer experiments.

Before moving a self-improvement trick to a new task, confirm that task offers the check the trick relies on, then test against a same-budget baseline.

California sued OpenAI, over that Hugging Face attack, representing one of the first major attempts to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident.

The lawsuit alleges OpenAI admitted losing control of its testing agents more than 80 times.

Attorney General Rob Bonta’s complaint, filed in San Francisco Superior Court, says OpenAI has publicly reported only 27 of them.

The case centers on July, when about 700 of its agents escaped a cybersecurity evaluation and attacked Hugging Face’s production systems.

They slipped out through a flaw in a misconfigured software-package server and took about 17,600 actions, yet OpenAI noticed nothing until Hugging Face disclosed the attack.

That blind spot anchors the deception claim of the lawsuit, since OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework requires 24x7 monitoring and network segmentation for High-capability models.

Bonta wants an injunction, restitution and civil penalties of $2,500 per violation under California’s unfair competition and public nuisance laws.

OpenAI’s technical report already conceded that guardrails it runs in production would have flagged the attack as unsafe.

If the court treats harm during internal testing as an unfair business practice, that will basically mean that state attorneys general can police every lab’s evaluation sandbox.

note_tweet.text:
New Huawei paper finds that code-evolution agents do better and spend less when search planning, code writing, and scoring are handled by 3 separate owners.

AlphaEvolve-style systems improve programs by writing code, scoring it, and picking what to try next. Some give the code writer little freedom, others let 1 coding agent steer the search at high token cost, and none hides the scorer.

EvoTrias gives each job its own owner. A controller steers the search, a coding agent like Claude Code writes code, and an evaluator the agent cannot read scores it.

On 7 math tasks it led 6 and cut token cost per run by 64% versus 4-agent CORAL. On OR-Tools, a 680K-line C++ repository, it lifted solver quality 13.2% on 300 instances, while 1-shot runs of the same agent averaged -0.1%.

For code-optimizing agent loops, hide the scorer from the agent and keep search planning out of the coding agent.

note_tweet.text:
New Carnegie Mellon paper finds that AI assistants that plan trips and shopping find more options people would accept by showing them a few real choices than by asking about their preferences.

A travel request like “restaurants rated 3.8 or higher” throws out a cheaper place rated 3.7 that the user would happily pick. People rarely say they would accept a lower rating to save money, because they only realize it when they see the actual options.

> Adding that 1 hidden trade-off to the request raised the share of plans the user accepted from 12% to 55%, with the same planner.

> Current agents (Claude Code, Gemini CLI and others) mostly asked questions and rarely showed plans, so they caught at most 32% of plans the user would accept.

> Agents that showed plans did clearly better than agents that asked.

When your agent turns a request into a plan, show the user a few options outside their stated limits early, before locking the spec.

Announcing Artificial Analysis Time to First Audio, measuring how quickly Text to Speech models start speaking. Among the leading models the wait ranges from 76 ms to nearly a second

Our Text to Speech benchmarks already cover quality, pronunciation and generation speed, but not how long a user waits before hearing anything — the number that decides whether a voice agent feels responsive. We measure every model daily on the same 12 prompts across four input lengths, timing audible speech rather than the first byte, and report a rolling 7-day mean.

Key results:

➤ Fastest at the frontier: @SpeechifyAI's Simba 3.5 starts in 116 ms — the highest Arena Elo of any model that begins speaking in under 200 ms. @InworldAI's Realtime TTS-2 follows at 186 ms.

➤ Turbo variants earn their name: @ElevenLabs' Eleven v4 Turbo starts in 258 ms against 653 ms for Eleven v4, at the same Arena Elo. @FishAudio's Fish Audio Drama 3 matches it at 258 ms and @cartesia's Sonic 3.6 is at 287 ms.

➤ Streaming is the dividing line: The 65 streaming models typically begin speaking within a few hundred milliseconds, a median of 376 ms. The 20 non-streaming models must finish generating before they return anything: a median of 2.0 seconds.

See more details below ⬇️

Can Python be a chatbot?

Over one week, we challenged a swarm of 1,000 agents to build one entirely in Python: no weights, no training, just a million rules :)

Each agent was an instance of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash that worked on different parts of the bot's conversational capabilities: understanding, answers, memory, routing, etc. 

They coordinated on a Slack-like message board we built for agents, wrote ~175k messages to each other, and merged ~8k PRs on a shared repo (which almost broke the Hub 🙈)

The result is PyBot: 630k lines of Python, zero dependencies, and on par with SmolLM-360M at answering everday questions. Just don't expect it to solve a Millennium Prize problem anytime soon :)

Code & demo: https://t.co/J52376WBsi
